sources.note: Wordlist forms only; no prosodic annotation.

sources.citation: Moran, Steven & McCloy, Daniel (eds). 2019. PHOIBLE 2.0, inventory 2748 'Mithaka (ER 2748)', contributed by Erich Round from Breen, Gavan. n.d. Mithaka [unpublished manuscript].
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: PHOIBLE records segments only (29: six-place stops with a fortis/lenis-type diacritic split, nasals, laterals, r, trill, glides, vowels i u o a); no tone segments listed; PHOIBLE has no stress field. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Breen, Gavan. 2004. Innamincka Talk: a grammar of the Innamincka dialect of Yandruwandha with notes on other dialects. Pacific Linguistics 558.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL7101.Y36 B74 2004)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL7101.Y36 B74 2004
sources.note: Grammar of the best-described Central Karnic neighbour (Yandruwandha); cited by the ISO 2012-020 request as context for Karuwali. Would supply a proxy statement for the subgroup, not for Karuwali itself.

sources.citation: Bowern, Claire. 2001. Karnic classification revisited. In J. Simpson, D. Nash, M. Laughren, P. Austin & B. Alpher (eds), Forty years on: Ken Hale and Australian languages, 245-261. Pacific Linguistics 512.
sources.note: Karuwali explicitly excluded: pp. 247-248 'The possibly Karnic languages not included here due to lack of materials are Birria (pirriya); Pirlatapa; Kungkari and Kungatutyi; Karendala, Karuwali and Kulumali..'. Only stress remark is a family-level aside in a pronoun etymology, p. 253: '(stress at all stages of Karnic is on the initial syllable of the word)' -- not a description of Karuwali.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid record karr1236 (Hammarstrom et al.).
sources.note: Glottolog's most extensive description = Anonymous 1886 (a wordlist or less); zero descriptive references; classification refs only (Breen 2007; Bowern 2010; Bowern & Atkinson 2012).

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Karuwali language' (en), accessed 2026-09-17.
sources.note: Classification only (dialect of Mithaka per Dixon 2002; Breen 2007; Bowern 2001); no phonology or stress.

sources.citation: Nash, David. 2025. Where strange words fit: Channelling Alice Duncan-Kemp. In Carmel O'Shannessy, James Gray & Denise Angelo (eds), Projecting Voices: Studies in Language and Linguistics in Honour of Jane Simpson, 613-682. Canberra: ANU Press. doi:10.22459/PV.2025.20
sources.note: No phonology beyond a 'Spelling conventions' section on how English-based spellings render the lamino-palatal stop, velar stop and low vowel; word-by-word etymological commentary (Pitta-Pitta copies from Roth 1897 vs genuine local Karuwali/Mithaka words). Identifies 'W.H.W.' as William Henry Watson of Currawilla and points to Nash 2022 (Zenodo transcription), Breen 1968-70 MS 121 and PARADISEC-type Mithaka materials. Nothing on stress, accent or tone.

sources.citation: Nash, David. 2022. Currungulla vocabulary. Zenodo dataset, doi:10.5281/zenodo.5827466 [spreadsheet transcription of W. H. W(atson). 1912. Currungulla tribal dialect. Science of Man 13(10): 211; 13(11): 231; 13(12): 251, with regularised forms and Austin 1990 proto-Karnic comparanda].
sources.note: Bare 75-item English-Currungulla wordlist (ngappa 'water', turroo 'fire', coonkoo 'head', tinna 'foot', curna 'man', punja 'woman', barcooloo 'two'..); no accent marks, no prose on pronunciation. Wordlist-only data, not a statement.

sources.note: Nothing; sources cited are classificatory only (Dixon 2002, Oates 1975, O'Grady et al. 1966, Walsh 1981, Wurm 1972/1994, Tindale 1974, Bowern 2001, Breen 2004 Innamincka Talk).

sources.citation: Breen, Gavan. 1997. Taps, stops & trills. In Darrell Tryon & Michael Walsh (eds), Boundary Rider: essays in honour of Geoffrey O'Grady, 71-93. Pacific Linguistics C-136. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Segmental only: argues from the old spellings that Karruwali, like Mithaka, had a stop voicing contrast and trill-released apical stops (dr/tr spellings), probably with borrowing from Yandruwandha/Yawarrawarrka. For Mithaka (own recordings): voicing distinction 'in perhaps all stop positions', apico-alveolar and retroflex trill-released stops, trill, tap and glide. The paper's stress mentions (pp. 73, 81-83: contrasts counted 'after the primary stressed (first) vowel') concern Djabugay, Yandruwandha and other languages' frequency counts, not Karruwali or Mithaka. No statement of Karruwali wor…

sources.citation: Austin, Peter. 1990. Classification of Lake Eyre languages. La Trobe Working Papers in Linguistics 3: 171-201.
sources.note: Places Karuwali in Central Karnic with Yandruwandha, Yawarrawarrka and Mithaka (AUSTLANG L35); lexicostatistic classification only.

sources.citation: Breen, Gavan. 1990. Salvage studies of western Queensland Aboriginal languages. Pacific Linguistics B-105. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: No chapter on Karruwali. p. vii lists its only sources as 'Karruwali (Anonymous 1886; W.R.W. 1912)'; bibliography p. 164: 'W.H.W., 1912, Currungulla tribal dialect. Science of Man 13/10:211; 13/11:231; 13/12:251'. Pirriya chapter (p. 8, p. 40) mentions Karruwali speakers Sally Flash and Morney Donald but gives no Karruwali data.

sources.citation: Breen, J. G. 1971. Aboriginal languages of western Queensland (preliminary version). Linguistic Communications 5: 1-88. Monash University.
sources.note: Nothing. Entry 16 'Karuwali' (p. ~9-10): 'Curr (Vol. II, p 371-3) has a wordlist in the language spoken by the "Karawalla" and "Tunberri" tribes, and a word-list in "Currungulla" was sent to Science of Man by a correspondent identified only as W.H.W.' Breen never recorded a speaker; Table 4 gives cognate counts only.

sources.citation: Schmidt, Wilhelm. 1912. Die Gliederung der australischen Sprachen (Fortsetzung). II. Teil: Die linguistische Gliederung der australischen Staemme. Anthropos 7: 463-497 [pp. 487-489: 'Die Karawalla-Tunberri-Sprache'].
sources.note: Twelve-word lexical comparison (Kopf, Auge, Zunge, Ohr, Haut, Hund, Emu, Fliege, Feuer, Erde, Stein) with Yarrawurka, Dieri, Evelyn Creek, Nulla; source list. No Lautlehre, nothing on Betonung/Akzent.

sources.citation: Anonymous. 1886. No. 106 'Lower Diamantina' (Karawalla and Tunberri tribes). In E. M. Curr, The Australian Race, vol. II, pp. 371-373. Melbourne: Govt Printer.
sources.note: Nothing. Half-page ethnographic note (monogamy, boomerang, circumcision) plus ~120-item wordlist in Curr's standard order; no remark on accent, stress or pronunciation. This is the sole primary datum Glottolog lists (Glottolog's fullest description is only a wordlist).

sources.citation: AIATSIS. AUSTLANG entry L35 Karuwali.
sources.note: Nothing. Documentation: Word list 'Less than 20 pages' (score 1); Text collection none; Grammar none; Audio-visual none. Comment: Bowern (2001) 'insufficient data'; Breen 1976:745 puts Garwali in a dialect chain with Ngamini, Midhaga, Dhirari, Dieri, Yaluyandi.
